extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft guidance for writing and revising fiction and poetry, emphasizing revision, clarity of intention, work ethic, and precise diction; aimed at writers developing their practice and preparing work for readers and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewriting: remove everything that is not the story
rubrics_metrics.description: "When you rewrite, your main job is taking out all the things that are not the story."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gould's central editorial rule: identify the core of the story and cut anything that doesn't serve it. Example from Gould's edits: he 'only took out the bad parts' rather than trying to add new material. Scoring/anti-patterns: overwritten passages, digressions, and gratuitous asides that distract from the narrative are precisely what revision should excise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write with the door closed; rewrite with the door open
rubrics_metrics.description: "Write with the door closed, rewrite with the door open."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First drafts are for the writer alone—get the material down without pandering to readers. Once you know what the story is, open it to readers, critics, and editors during revision. Be prepared to accept criticism and to make changes; the piece 'belongs to anyone who wants to read it. Or criticize it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell yourself the story first
rubrics_metrics.description: "When you write a story, you're telling yourself the story."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write primarily to discover and tell the story to yourself honestly; authenticity in the draft helps create a coherent narrative. This internal clarity makes subsequent revision more effective because you already know what you meant to do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and be able to explain your work
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer should know what they meant to say — Tabby 'knew exactly what she had meant to say, and had said most of it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In workshops and editorial contexts, being able to explicate your intentions, references, and choices demonstrates craft and control. Example: Tabby's poem showed knowledge of Augustine and her own symbolic choices; that understanding strengthened readers' responses. Anti-pattern: writers who cannot articulate purpose or meaning when pressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work ethic: craft matters more than mythic spontaneous inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the notion that 'good writing came spontaneously ... writers were blessed stenographers taking divine dictation.' Instead, writing requires steady labor: 'writing poems (or stories, or essays) had as much in common with sweeping the floor as with mythy moments of revelation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value daily practice, discipline, and the meticulousness of craft over waiting for sudden epiphanies. The text contrasts sloppy, aura-based notions of creativity with poems that combine intoxicating feeling and idea-driven craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague, general abstractions (use concrete, precise diction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of poems that rely on generalized words: 'If the resulting poem is sloppy, based on the assumption that such general words as "loneliness" mean the same thing to all of us...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concrete, specific imagery and diction over broad abstractions that assume shared meaning. Anti-pattern/example: the mock poem in the chapter that uses fractured, vague lines ('I close my eyes / in th dark I see ... loneliness') — an example of how abstraction can produce sloppiness and incomprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let good editing prune rather than over-explain
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial approach exemplified by Gould: 'I only took out the bad parts, you know. Most of it’s pretty good.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust that cutting weak material often strengthens a piece more than adding explanation. Be willing to have editors (or your own ruthless revision) remove superfluous passages rather than over-elaborate to justify them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional and practical support sustains a writing life
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Having someone who believes in you makes a lot of difference.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges the non-craft elements necessary for sustained productivity: supportive partners, friends, or peers who believe in the writer can help maintain motivation through difficult periods. This is a pragmatic criterion for long-term creative success rather than a textual one.
